You can certainly cherry pick reviews of his that "got it wrong", but he is considered one of the greatest film critics for a reason.  He loved film, he loved writing about film, and he reviewed in a way that a lot of people connected with.

I’m not going to defend any individual critic, but I think there is an important aspect that is being overlooked. The expectation of what a movie is and who made it are important aspects to take into account when writing a review. That isn’t to say that the greatest movies made in a year are dependent on that criteria, but good reviewers don’t review in a vacuum because they want their readers to understand their perspective.

My favorite example of this is The Irishman, because it is so well known and Scorsese is such a well established director. I would start a review of The Irishman by stating that it is a fantastic movie, maybe one of the best of the year it came out. But I would continue to proceed by pointing out some of its flaws. Not because it is a bad movie or I want to crap on Scorsese, but because he is one of the most talented directors in the world and readers have an idea in their head that when they think “a Scorsese film that is one of this years best.” 

The other important reason to emphasize it with The Irishman, and this comes down to my personal opinion, is that even though it was one of that year’s best movies, it wasn’t s not one of the best movies of all time. That important when you are talking about a Scorsese movie because, again my opinion, his high water mark has given us some of the greatest movies of all time and sugar coating a flawed but terrific movie like The Irishman diminishes what we hold up to be best in movies.

On the flip side, if The Irishman was a director’s first movie, it would be a disservice to the readers to emphasize the flaws. No baseline being established, I would only mention them in passing and enthusiastically focus on the accomplishment.

You’re probably barking up the wrong tree on this sub since most of our viewing habits probably align with that of people who’s profession it is to do so, but I take issue with the idea that critics are inherently “biased” because they watch too many movies, as of there’s some kind of limit to what you can watch before it changes you, and I would argue this is especially true where film has become so commonplace that viewing habits are probably high across the board. 

Ebert is one of the great pop film critics of all time and his defense of his negative reviews shouldn’t be held as a negative, like it’s a fixation. 

And it’s a commonly touted point against critics that they become apathetic after watching too much and being forced to watch things that they don’t care about, but in my experience, this isn’t really actually true in a meaningful way. Many critics don’t review things that don’t actually appeal to them, and many critics engage with film in a respectable way, even if it isn’t their cup of tea. 

Lastly, anti-critic sentiment always seems to stem from reactionary immediate emotions about films by which people have a vested interest in, and while I empathize with that, I’ve yet to actually see a meaningful trend that critics (which aren’t a monolith but that’s a separate issue) by design are totally wrong about film or have an inverse reaction to what common discourse is. Notable exceptions are films like The Thing, but it’s rare. And I feel now more than ever that critics are willing to write on the level that the film asks for, leading most critics today to generally lean more positive than negative.

Here is my belief and my belief only.

Genre burnout is a thing.

Is someone who watches more movies more likely to burn out in a genre?

Absolutely.

I think the frustrating thing is that the burnout could probably conceptually be in any movie.

So if a film critic who is burned out on superhero movies watches Iron Man 3.. I doubt there would be this newfound rekindling of the love toward that genre.

I personally think that it's one of those things that may take a while to kind of reinvigorate that passion.

But I also think that when you have audiences who don't watch movies, I believe it kind of allows Hollywood to go into their old playbook because it's not being tracked. 

An easy thing to think about is the MGM Garland vehicle The Wizard of Oz is erroneously considered to be the first color film by quite a few members of the general public. 

I don't quite think that that's the worst misperception.

The adventures of Prince Ahmed is a feature length film that is both animated and in color during the late silent period.

But what I think is happening is that the formulas of yesterday are now kind of evolving to the CGI setpieces of today. 

And so for me maybe critics are hi't miss on how they review movies, but perhaps the overlining is that they can point to films that have original overarching stories. 

I don't think that's a bad thing.

I feel as though OP is misdiagnosing the role of a critic as it’s taken nowadays to be one of giving an objective, complete view, review and appraisal of a worthy work when it should be much more to hear a very specific and individual  take as establishes a consistent voice. I find it a strange choice to pursue what a specific critic has to say when they clearly are not interested in, or in saying anything interesting about the subject of their critique.

The best critics, much like the best work that can be approached, are idiosyncratic, and should, I think, lead with their clear biases so that you know their margin of error. My method is to approach a specific review/writing with that foreknowledge that necessarily, a critic has their preferences and foibles, and I think that so long as they are able to make good points and talk about what they’d like to, there is a certain amount of stranger/more perfunctory takes that can be dismissed because they are dismissible.

That said, I would hope that a critic would not be immune to having genuine moments with films despite their going-in impressions.

Like Mick LaSalle of the SF Chronicle trashed Attack the Block because it opens with a group of kids who rob a nurse on her way home from work. Those kids are the film's protagonists. This is his exact quote:

"Some unsolicited advice: If you're going to show people imperiled by aliens, make us care whether said people live or die. Or at the very least don't make your audience actively root for the aliens by showing your ostensible heroes mugging a young woman at knifepoint in the movie's first scene. I imagine you must think I'm exaggerating, but no. The characters we're expected to engage with, the people for whom our rooting interest is simply assumed, are violent street thugs. Sorry, I'm with the aliens on this one."

Do you know how idiotic that is? The young woman is the audience surrogate. She ends up grouped up with the kids. Initially, she doesn't like them—because they robbed her. But over the course of the film, she gets to know them and comes to understand how difficult their lives are. They all have struggling families and are mostly on their own, caring for each other. Her anger turns to empathy turns to genuine compassion. Which is the exact journey the audience is supposed to go on. 

Except Mick doesn't get that. Why? Because he doesn't understand narrative. He's a critic who has watched thousands of movies but doesn't actually understand what he's writing about. 

It's kind of like architecture. All of us are in buildings all of the time. But it doesn't mean we understand the first thing about how those buildings are made or the design choices that went into them. 

Imagine someone with absolutely know background in architecture giving you a tour of a building. That's what most film critics are. 

A lot of them mean well and try to give a thoughtful evaluation. But too many think they're superior to the movies they watch and that we're lucky to be hearing what they have to say about it.

When a movie is reminiscent of something done 43 years ago, it’s more of an homage.   Another example is “Chinatown,” a neo-noir that harkened back to the cinema of the 1940’s.

“Taxi Driver,” itself, has elements of the Western and the 40’s noir.

All this to say that “Joker” is hardly a cheap carbon copy of typical contemporary filmmaking.  It excited me precisely because it reminds me of cinema of the 1970’s and even of 1967’s “Bonnie and Clyde.”

Calling “Joker” plagiarized is a very strong epithet.   Murnau’s silent masterpiece “Nosferatu” *was* blatantly plagiarized — from Bram Stoker’s “Dracula.” So much so that Stoker’s widow sued.

Strongly influenced by, in homage to, a remake of, is far more judicious a description than a plagiarization. Except that I wouldn’t even call “Joker” even close to being a remake of anything.

As I mentioned in another post, “Taxi Driver” has elements of the American Western and of 40’s noir.   The film “Chinatown” was a neo-noir and not, let’s say, a plagiarization of a 40’s noir style and theme.   

A pastiche is another term one could add to the movie-influence lexicon.  To hold the director of “Joker” to a more rigorous standard than that of other filmmakers — for whatever reason, including in the vein of “where does he get off addressing himself to the canon of great cinema?” —  would be unfair.
And if you watch/read any interviews with Philips he didn't deny them. He embraced them.

Throwaway was referring to its having won the Golden Lion in Venice and the Golden Frog in Poland.   Global acclaim would have been a more apt description.

The jury of Venice, no doubt, was familiar with the films of Scorsese and didn’t consider the influence or homage element, nor the pastiche of 70’s filmmaking, to be incriminating.  

Not to mention that the Scorsese influence in “Joker” was organic insofar as DeNiro (who *starred* in Taxi Driver, for God’s sake) signed on to the project.   Insofar as he was, he himself was a creative contributor.   Scorsese, himself, was originally slated to produce.  

By analogy,  “Halloween” features Jamie Lee Curtis, daughter of Janet Leigh of “Psycho” fame and, as did “Psycho,” features a character named Sam Loomis. 

When influences, including influences from a bygone *era*, are present, cinephiles tend to get excited.   The jury at Venice apparently did and this was removed from the politicized wrangling that surrounded the film in America.

It literally won awards in festivals all over the world, including the Oscars. And it made 1 billion in box office as an R rated movie. I don't know how you can put a Rotten Tomatoes score above all of these.
